(p. 462)

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Najm (The Star)

God, exalted is He, says: ﴿By the star when it sets﴾ ﴿your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾ ﴿nor does he speak from [his own] desire﴾ ﴿it is not but a revelation revealed﴾.

The scholars differed about what is meant by this star by which God swore in this noble verse. Some said that it refers to the star with which the devils are stoned. Others said that it refers to the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), which is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and others. The word "najm" (star) is a proper name for the Pleiades by predominance, so the Arabs hardly use the word "najm" unqualified except to refer to them. From this is the saying of Nabigha Dhubyani:

"I say, while the star's last part has leaned toward setting, look once and be steadfast, O one who is perplexed."

So his saying "by the star" means the Pleiades.

God's saying ﴿when it sets﴾ means: when it falls at dawn. This is the view chosen by Ibn Jarir. It was also said that "al-najm" is Venus (al-Zuhrah). It was said that the intended meaning of "al-najm" is the stars of the sky. On this view, it is the use of the singular to mean the plural, like God's saying ﴿and they will turn their backs﴾ [al-Qamar: 45], meaning the backs. And His saying ﴿and your Lord comes, and the angel [comes] in rows upon rows﴾ [al-Fajr: 22], meaning the angels. And His saying ﴿those will be rewarded with the high chamber for what they endured﴾ [al-Furqan: 75], meaning the chambers.

We have already presented many examples of this in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs, in the commentary on God's saying ﴿then We bring you forth as a child﴾ [al-Hajj: 5] in Surah al-Hajj. The use of "najm" to mean the stars in the plural is well known in the language. From it is the saying of 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah:

"Then they said, 'You love her.' I said, 'Indeed' ∗∗∗ as many as the stars, the pebbles, and the dust."

And the saying of al-Ra'i:

"So she spent the night counting the stars, in a crouching, cold place, whose camels' humps were..."

(p. 463) On this view, the meaning of the stars' falling is their setting, or their scattering on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said that "al-najm" is the plant that has no stalk. Some scholars said that the intended meaning of "al-najm" is the portion of the Qur'an that was sent down, for it was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ in installments over twenty-three years. Each portion of it, at the time of its revelation, is truly called "najm" in correct Arabic usage, just as the term is applied to a blood-money installment that has come due from the 'aqilah (paternal kin who bear blood money), and to a mukatab slave's installment payment.

On this view, God's saying ﴿when it falls﴾ means: when the angel descended with it from the sky to the Prophet ﷺ. As for the verb "hawa," yahwi huwiyyan, it means that it cut through the air descending from above to below.

Know first that the view that it is the Pleiades, and that "al-najm" refers specifically to them, though it was chosen by Ibn Jarir and transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas and more than one other, is not, in my view, sound (wajih).

The more apparent view is that "al-najm" refers to the stars in the plural. Ibn Jarir said that this is not correct, but the proof for it is God's use of the plural "stars" in the oath in His saying ﴿so I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 75], because the apparent meaning of "the star when it sets" here is the same as the meaning of "the positions of the stars" in al-Waqi'ah.

The scholars also differed about the meaning of "the positions of the stars." Some said they are their places of setting when they go down. Some said they are their scattering on the Day of Resurrection. Some said they are their locations in the sky, because what descends is located in a place. Some said they are the positions of the stars of the Qur'an, which the angel brought down to the Prophet ﷺ.

The one who wrote these notes, may God pardon and forgive him, says: The view that is most apparent to me and closest to the truth in my judgment is that what is meant by "the star when it sets" here in this surah, and by "the positions of the stars" in al-Waqi'ah, is the stars of the Qur'an, which the angel brought down star by star. This is for two reasons:

The first: What God swore about by "the star when it sets" is that the Prophet ﷺ is upon the truth, that he has not strayed, nor erred, and that he does not speak from desire, but it is only a revelation revealed. This is consistent in meaning with what He swore about by "the positions of the stars," which is His saying ﴿indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾ ﴿in a protected Book﴾ up to His saying ﴿a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 77–80].

(p. 464) The swearing by the Qur'an to confirm the validity of the Prophet's ﷺ mission and the truthfulness of the great Qur'an, and that it was sent down from God, is explained in verses of God's Book, such as His saying ﴿Ya-Sin﴾ ﴿by the wise Qur'an﴾ ﴿indeed you are among the messengers﴾ ﴿upon a straight path﴾ ﴿a revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin: 1–5], and His saying ﴿Ha-Mim﴾ ﴿by the clear Book﴾ ﴿indeed We have made it an Arabic Qur'an, that you may understand﴾ ﴿and indeed it is in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and wise﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 1–4]. The best way to interpret the Qur'an is by the Qur'an.

The second: That the sworn-by thing described as "stars" is the great Qur'an is more fitting to His saying after it: ﴿and indeed it is a great oath, if you only knew﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 76], because this glorification by God indicates that the thing sworn by is of the utmost greatness.

There is no doubt that the Qur'an, which is the speech of God, is more fitting for that than the stars of the sky and the star of the earth. And God knows best.

As for His saying, in this noble verse, ﴿your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾: some scholars said: going astray (al-dalal) occurs from ignorance of the truth, while erring (al-ghayy) is deviating from the truth while knowing it. That is, he did not ignore the truth nor deviate from it; rather, he knows the truth and follows it.

We have already presented the uses of "al-dalal" in the Qur'an, with their Arabic evidence, in the commentary on Surah al-Shu'ara' concerning God's saying ﴿he said, "I did it then, and I was among those who are astray"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 20], and in Surah al-Kahf concerning God's saying ﴿Say: Shall we inform you of the greatest losers in deeds? ﴾ ﴿those whose effort is lost in the life of this world﴾ and the verse following [al-Kahf: 103–104].

What this noble verse includes regarding his ﷺ being upon the straight guidance is explained in many verses of God's Book:

• such as His saying ﴿so rely upon God; indeed you are upon the manifest truth﴾ [al-Naml: 79],

• and His saying ﴿so let them not dispute with you in the matter; and invite to your Lord; indeed you are upon a straight guidance﴾ [al-Hajj: 67],

• and His saying ﴿and indeed you guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura: 52].

We have already presented the verses clarifying this in Surah al-Zukhruf, in the commentary on God's saying ﴿so hold firmly to that which has been revealed to you; indeed you are upon a straight path﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 43]. As for His saying in this noble verse, ﴿it is not but a revelation revealed﴾, the scholars of usul al-fiqh (the principles of jurisprudence) used it as evidence that the Prophet ﷺ did not exercise ijtihad (independent reasoning). Those who said that he could exercise ijtihad argued

(p. 465) • from His saying ﴿God has pardoned you; why did you grant them permission?﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Tawbah: 43],

• and His saying ﴿it is not for a prophet to have captives until he has inflicted a massacre upon the land﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Anfal: 67],

• and His saying ﴿it is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Tawbah: 113].

They said: If this had not been from ijtihad, He would not have said ﴿God has pardoned you; why did you grant them permission?﴾ up to the end of the verse, nor would He have said ﴿it is not for a prophet to have captives.﴾ There is no contradiction between the verses, because His saying ﴿it is not but a revelation revealed﴾ means that the Prophet ﷺ conveys from God only what God has revealed to him to convey. Whoever says that he is a poet, a magician, a soothsayer, or the fables of the ancients is the greatest liar and most disbelieving of God's creation. This does not contradict his having granted permission to those who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk, his taking captives on the day of Badr, and his asking forgiveness for his uncle Abu Talib without a specific revelation coming down to him about that. We have explained this at length in another place.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 53, verse 3:

The author said in (Dafʿ Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

(p-402) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat an-Najm (The Star)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor does he speak from [his own] desire. It is not but a revelation revealed.﴾

This noble verse indicates, by its apparent meaning, that the Prophet (ﷺ) does not exercise ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) in anything. However, other verses have come indicating that he (ﷺ) may have exercised ijtihad in some matters, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah pardon you. Why did you give them permission?﴾ [at-Tawbah: 43].

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not for a prophet to have captives until he inflicts a massacre upon the land﴾ — the verse [al-Anfal: 67].

The answer to this is in two respects:

The first: This is what Ibn Jarir restricted himself to, and what Ibn al-Hajib opened with in his concise work on usul al-fiqh (Mukhtasar al-Usuli): that the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor does he speak from [his own] desire﴾ is: in everything he conveys from Allah. ﴿It is not but a revelation revealed﴾ means: everything he conveys from Allah is nothing but revelation from Him, because he does not say anything about Allah except by revelation from Him. So the verse is a refutation of the disbelievers when they said that the Prophet (ﷺ) had fabricated this Qur'an, as Ibn al-Hajib said.

The second aspect: If he did exercise ijtihad, he exercised it only by revelation from Allah, Who permitted him to do that ijtihad. Accordingly, his ijtihad is by revelation, and there is no contradiction.

What supports this aspect is that his ijtihad in granting permission to those who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk was something Allah permitted him to do, when He said: ﴿So grant permission to whom you will among them﴾ [an-Nur: 62]. When he granted permission to the hypocrites, He rebuked him saying: ﴿Allah pardon you. Why did you give them permission until it became clear to you who were truthful and you knew the liars?﴾ [at-Tawbah: 43].

So the ijtihad in reality is merely granting permission before the distinction became clear, not permission in general, since it was stated explicitly in the text.

The question of the Prophet's (ﷺ) ijtihad and its absence is among the well-known disputed questions among the scholars of usul al-fiqh, (p-403) and the cause of their disagreement is the apparent conflict among the verses.

The one who restricts it (may Allah pardon him) said: What appears to be the correct position on this question is that the Prophet (ﷺ) at times did some matters without specific revelation concerning them, such as his granting permission to those who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk before it became clear to him who among them was truthful and who was lying, and his taking captives at Badr, and his command to stop pollinating the palm trees, and his saying: "Had I known at the start of my affair what I came to know at its end, I would not have..." (the hadith "If I had faced from my matter what I have turned away from"), and so on.

As for the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor does he speak from [his own] desire﴾, there is no difficulty in it, because the Prophet (ﷺ) does not speak anything out of desire, nor does he talk according to desire.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not but a revelation revealed﴾ means that everything he conveys from Allah is revelation from Allah, not by desire, nor by lying, nor by fabrication. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

al-Shinqiti's commentary (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 53, verse 5:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He has been taught by one mighty in power﴾.

What is meant by "one mighty in power" (shadid al-quwa) in this verse is Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him. The meaning is that the Prophet ﷺ was taught this revelation by an angel mighty in power, namely Jibril.

This noble verse contains two matters:

The first: that this revelation, of which this great Qur'an is the greatest part, was taught to the Prophet ﷺ by Jibril, by command from Allah.

The second: that Jibril is greatly powerful.

These two matters have come clarified in other places.

As for the first of them, namely that Jibril descended to him with this revelation and taught it to him, it has come clarified in verses of the Book of Allah, such as:

• His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Jibril – indeed, he has brought it down upon your heart by the permission of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 97], and the rest of the verse.

• His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds. The trustworthy Spirit has brought it down, upon your heart, that you may be among the warners﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 192–194].

• His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114]. (p-466) And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation. So when We have recited it, follow its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16–18].

That is: when the angel sent to you with it from Us, conveying it on Our behalf, recites it to you, ﴿then follow its recitation﴾, i.e., recite as you heard it being recited.

As for the second matter, namely the great strength of Jibril who descends with this revelation, He mentioned it in His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, one mighty, with standing before the Lord of the Throne, secure﴾ [at-Takwir: 19–20]. His saying in this verse of at-Takwir, ﴿the word of a messenger﴾, means: the word conveyed by him from Allah. The mention of "messenger" indicates that he only conveys what he has been sent with. So the speech is the speech of Allah in its words and its meanings, and Jibril is a conveyor from Allah; and in this sense the speech is attributed to him, because the Prophet ﷺ heard it only from him. It is thus the word which Allah sent with him and commanded him to convey, as the indication of the mention of "messenger" shows. The clarification of this issue will come, Allah willing, in the commentary on surah at-Takwir. And knowledge is with Allah, may He be exalted.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The eye did not swerve, nor did it transgress.﴾

We have already presented some discussion of this in the beginning of Surat al-Isra'.

Allah's saying: ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ ﴿That, then, would be an unjust division.﴾

We have already presented, at length, the verses that clarify this matter in Surat an-Nahl, in the discussion of His saying: ﴿And they assign to Allah daughters﴾ [an-Nahl 16:57], and in several other passages of this blessed Book.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So to Allah belongs the Hereafter and the First.﴾

In this noble verse, He, majestic and exalted, made clear that the Hereafter and the First belong to Him, and that the First is this world, al-dunya (the present life). He made this clear in another place, in His saying: ﴿Indeed, upon Us is guidance﴾ ﴿and indeed to Us belong the Hereafter and the First﴾ [al-Layl: 12]. In another place He made clear that everything belongs to Him, in His saying: ﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, who has made it sacred, and to whom belongs everything﴾ [al-Naml: 91]. This is among what is known of the religion by necessity.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 53, verse 26:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And how many angels are there in the heavens whose intercession will avail nothing except after Allah gives permission to whom He wills and approves.﴾

We have already presented the verses that clarify this in Surat al-Baqarah, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: (p-467) ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48], and in other places.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾.

We have also already presented the verses that clarify it in Surat al-Zukhruf, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, into females﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19], and in other places.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 53, verse 31:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, that He may recompense those who did evil with what they did and recompense those who did good with the best﴾.

We have already presented the verses that clarify this in Surah al-Ahqaf, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except in truth and for a specified term﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 3], and in Surah adh-Dhariyat, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 56].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 53, verse 32:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who avoid major sins and immoralities, except for minor faults﴾.

We have already presented the verses that clarify this in Surah ash-Shura, in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who avoid major sins and immoralities, and when they are angry, they forgive﴾ [ash-Shura: 37].

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He brought you forth from the earth, and when you were embryos in the wombs of your mothers. So do not claim purity for yourselves﴾.

We have already presented the verses that clarify this in Surah an-Nisa', in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves? Rather, Allah purifies whom He wills﴾ [an-Nisa': 49], and in other places besides that.

[p. 468] Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Have you seen the one who turned away,﴾ ﴿and gave a little and then held back?﴾ ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen, so that he sees?﴾ ﴿Or has he not been informed of what is in the scrolls of Musa,﴾ ﴿and of Ibrahim, who fulfilled [his duty],﴾ ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another,﴾ ﴿and that man has only what he strives for,﴾ ﴿and that his striving will be seen,﴾ ﴿then he will be repaid for it with the fullest recompense.﴾

His saying "tawalla" means he turned back and withdrew from the truth. As for His saying "wa a'ta qalilan" (﴿and gave a little﴾), some said: a little of wealth. Others said: he gave a little of good speech. His saying "wa akda" (﴿and held back﴾) means he cut off that giving and did not complete it. Its origin is from the phrase "akda sahib al-hafr" (the digger reached a rock), when, in his digging, he reached a rock he could not dig through. Its root is from "al-kudya," which is the stones that obstruct the digger of a well or the like and prevent him from digging.

Regarding the one who "gave a little and held back," the scholars differed. It was said that he is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, who came close to believing in the Prophet (ﷺ). Some of the polytheists rebuked him, saying: "Have you abandoned the religion of your elders and led them astray?" He said: "I feared the punishment of Allah." So the one who rebuked him guaranteed that, if he gave him a certain amount of his wealth and returned to his polytheism, he would bear the punishment of Allah on his behalf. Al-Walid then returned to polytheism, gave the one who had rebuked him some of that wealth he had guaranteed, and withheld the rest. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed the verse.

Based on this, His saying "tawalla" means al-Walid turned away from Islam after he had come close to it. "Gave a little of wealth" means to the one who guaranteed to bear his sins on his behalf. "Wa akda" means he was stingy toward him with the remainder. It was also said: he gave a little of good speech, such as praising the Qur'an and acknowledging the truthfulness of the Prophet (ﷺ), and "wa akda" means he stopped and turned back from that.

It was also said that he is al-As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi. He sometimes agreed with the Prophet (ﷺ) on some matters, and that is the meaning of his giving a little and then stopping, which is the meaning of his holding back. This is the saying of al-Suddi, but it does not harmonize with what follows: ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen…﴾ to the end of the verse [an-Najm: 35].

It is narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that he was Abu Jahl. He said: "By Allah, Muhammad (ﷺ) only commands us to noble character," and that is the meaning of his giving a little, while his cutting off from that is well known.

Al-Zamakhshari confined himself to the view that it is Uthman ibn Affan (may Allah be pleased with him). He said: It is narrated that Uthman ibn Affan used to give his wealth in good causes. Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh, who was his foster brother, said to him: "Soon nothing will remain for you." Uthman said: "I have sins and wrongdoings, and by what I do I seek the pleasure of Allah the Exalted and hope for His pardon." Abdullah said: "Give me your she-camel with its saddle, and I will bear all your sins on your behalf." So he gave it to him and had witnesses to it, and he withheld his giving, and the verse was revealed. The meaning of "tawalla" is that he abandoned his post on the day of Uhud. Then Uthman returned to what was better and more beautiful than that. End of quote from him.

This saying is not hidden to be weak and baseless, and it is unfitting for the rank of the Commander of the Faithful Uthman ibn Affan (may Allah be pleased with him).

These noble verses contain seven matters:

The first: the denial of knowledge of the unseen, indicated by the interrogative hamza in His saying ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen…﴾, and the intended meaning is the negation of his knowledge of the unseen.

The second: that for each of Ibrahim and Musa there are scrolls, of which this disbeliever has not been informed.

The third: that Ibrahim fulfilled, i.e., completed the performance of the duties which his Lord assigned to him.

The fourth: that in those scrolls is that ﴿no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾.

The fifth: that in them also is that ﴿man has only what he strives for﴾.

The sixth: ﴿and that his striving will be seen﴾.

The seventh: that he ﴿will be repaid for it with the fullest recompense﴾, i.e., the most complete and perfect.

All these seven matters have been clarified in other places.

As for the first of them, namely that they have no knowledge of the unseen, Allah mentioned it in many places, such as:

• His saying: ﴿Or do they have the unseen, so that they write it down?﴾ [al-Qalam: 47].
• His saying: ﴿Has he attained knowledge of the unseen, or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?﴾ [Maryam: 78].
• His saying: ﴿And Allah would not inform you of the unseen﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 179].
• His saying: ﴿He is the Knower of the unseen, and He does not reveal His unseen to anyone, except to a messenger whom He has approved﴾ [al-Jinn: 26].
• His saying: ﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾ [al-Naml: 65].

Verses of this kind are many and well known, and we have presented them repeatedly.

As for the second, which is that Ibrahim and Musa had scrolls of which this one who turned away, gave a little and held back, had no knowledge, Allah mentioned it in His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scrolls, the scrolls of Ibrahim and Musa﴾ [al-A'la: 18–19].

The third of them: that Ibrahim fulfilled his duties. Allah mentioned it in His saying: ﴿And when his Lord tested Ibrahim with words, and he fulfilled them﴾ [al-Baqara: 124]. We have previously stated that the most correct view regarding the "words" with which he was tested is that they are the duties.

As for the fourth: that ﴿no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, Allah mentioned it in verses of His Book, such as His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed: "Follow our way, and we will bear your sins." But they will never bear anything of their sins; indeed, they are liars﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 12], and His saying: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another. And if a heavily laden soul calls for help with its load, nothing of it will be carried, even by a near relative﴾ [Fatir: 18].

We have already presented the verses clarifying this, and the answer to the difficulty that arises from them was given in Surat Bani Isra'il when discussing His saying: ﴿No bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another, and We would never punish until We send a messenger﴾ [al-Isra': 15]. We also mentioned the way to reconcile the verses that come on this matter in Surat al-Nahl when discussing His saying: ﴿And some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge. Unquestionably, evil is what they bear﴾ [al-Nahl: 25].

As for the fifth: that ﴿man has only what he strives for﴾, it has come clarified in verses of the Book of Allah, such as:

• His saying: ﴿If you do good, you do good for your own souls; and if you do evil, it is against them﴾ [al-Isra': 7].
• His saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own self; and whoever does evil, it is against it﴾ [al-Jathiya: 15].
• His saying: ﴿And whoever does righteousness, they are preparing for themselves﴾ [al-Rum: 44].

Verses of this kind are many and well known.

His saying in this noble verse, ﴿and that man has only what he strives for﴾, indicates that a person does not deserve reward except for his own striving. This verse does not address whether he benefits from the striving of others, neither by negation nor by affirmation, because His saying ﴿and that man has only what he strives for﴾ has the particle "lam" (of possession) indicating that he does not deserve or possess anything except by his striving, and it does not address the negation of benefiting from what is not his possession nor something he deserves.

There is a verse in the Book of Allah indicating that a person may benefit from the striving of others, namely His saying: ﴿And those who believed and whose descendants followed them in faith – We will join with them their descendants, and We will not deprive them of anything of their deeds﴾ [al-Tur: 21].

We have clarified the way to reconcile His saying ﴿and that man has only what he strives for﴾ with His saying ﴿And those who believed and whose descendants followed them in faith﴾ and the rest of the verse, in our book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab" (Removing the Appearance of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book), in Surat al-Najm. There we said the following, and its text is: The answer is from three aspects:

The first: the verse only indicates the negation of a person's ownership of anything other than his striving; it does not indicate the negation of his benefiting from the striving of others, because He did not say: "And that man will never benefit except by what he strove for," but He said ﴿and that man has no...﴾, and there is a clear difference between the two matters. For the striving of another is the possession of its doer: if he wishes, he gives it to another, and that other benefits from it; and if he wishes, he keeps it for himself.

The scholars have agreed on the benefit the deceased receives from prayer over him, supplication for him, Hajj performed on his behalf, and the like, of what is established as benefit from the deeds of others.

The second: the faith of the descendants is the greatest cause for raising their ranks, for had they been disbelievers, that would not have been attained for them. The faith of the servant and his obedience is thus a striving on his part to benefit from the deeds of others among the Muslims, as occurs in prayer in congregation, for the prayer of some of them with others multiplies the reward compared to his praying alone. That multiplication is a benefit from the deed of another, for which the worshipper strove by his faith and his prayer in congregation. This aspect is indicated by His saying: ﴿and whose descendants followed them in faith﴾.

The third: the striving by which the raising of the children's ranks is achieved is not the children's own striving, as the text of His saying ﴿and that man has only what he strives for﴾ indicates; rather it is the striving of the parents, by which Allah delights their eyes, in that He raises their children to them so that they may enjoy seeing them in Paradise.

Thus the verse confirms the other and does not contradict it, for the intended purpose of the raising is the honouring of the parents, not of the children. The children's benefit is a consequence, and for them it is a favour from Allah which they did not earn, just as He bestowed that favour upon the youths, the wide-eyed maidens of Paradise, and the creatures He will create for Paradise. And knowledge is with Allah the Exalted. End of quote from him.

The sixth and seventh matters are that ﴿his striving will be seen﴾ and then ﴿he will be repaid for it with the fullest recompense﴾. Both have come clarified in many verses, such as His saying: ﴿And the weighing on that day is the truth. Those whose scales are heavy – it is they who will be successful. And those whose scales are light – those are the ones who have lost themselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 8–9], and His saying: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzala: 7–8], and His saying: ﴿And We will set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in anything. And if there is [an action] of the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it. And sufficient are We as reckoners﴾ [al-Anbiya': 47], and His saying: ﴿And We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a record which he will find laid open. [He will be told:] "Read your record; sufficient is yourself against you this Day as a accountant"﴾ [al-Isra': 13–14]. Verses of this kind are many and well known.

His saying in this noble verse, ﴿then his striving will be seen﴾, i.e., he knows that unseen. The verse indicates that the occasion of revelation does not exclude the giving of something in exchange for bearing the sins of the one who gave, because the doer of that does not have knowledge of the unseen, so he would know through it that the one who guaranteed to bear his sins by doing so was not informed of what is in the former scrolls, that ﴿no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, i.e., no soul bears the sin of another soul.

We have already presented its explanation clarified in Surat Bani Isra'il, and that a person does not possess nor deserve anything except his own striving. It has become clear from this that it is not possible for a person to bear the sins of another, and many well-known verses indicate this.

Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: "A-fa-ra'ayta" means "inform me," and the first object is the relative pronoun with its relative clause. The second object is the clause ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen, so that he sees?﴾.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 53, verse 39:

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that man will have nothing except what he strives for.﴾

This noble verse indicates that no one benefits from the deeds of another.

Another verse has come indicating that some people may benefit from the deeds of others, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who believed and whose descendants followed them in faith - We will join them with their descendants.﴾ [al-Tur: 21]. The raising of the ranks of the children, whether we say they are the adults or the young children, is a benefit obtained by them, and it was obtained by them through the deeds of their fathers, not through their own deeds.

Know first that what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, that this was a law for those before us, which was abrogated (naskh) in our law, is not correct. Rather, the verse "and that man will have nothing except what he strives for" is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated). Likewise, the claim that the intended meaning of "man" (al-insan) is specifically the disbeliever is also not correct.

The answer comes in three aspects:

The first: the verse only indicates the negation of a person's ownership of anything other than his own striving, and it does not indicate the negation of his benefiting from the striving of others, because it did not say "and that man will never benefit except from what he strove for," but said: "and that man has nothing." And there is a clear difference between the two matters, because the striving of another is the property of the one who strives: if he wishes, he gives it to another, and that other benefits from it; and if he wishes, he keeps it for himself.

The scholars have agreed on the deceased benefiting from the funeral prayer offered for him, from supplication for him, from Hajj performed on his behalf, and the like, in matters where benefit from the deeds of others has been established.

(p-404) The second: the faith of the descendants is the greatest cause of the raising of their ranks, for if they had been disbelievers, that would not have been obtained for them. Thus the faith of the servant and his obedience is a striving on his part to benefit from the deeds of others among the Muslims, as occurs in prayer in congregation: the prayer of some of them together with others multiplies the reward beyond his prayer alone. That multiplication is a benefit from the deed of another, toward which the worshipper strove through his faith and his prayer in congregation. This aspect is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and whose descendants followed them in faith﴾.

The third: the striving through which the raising of the ranks of the children was achieved is not the children's own, as is the explicit wording of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that man will have nothing except what he strives for.﴾ Rather, it is the striving of the fathers. It is a striving for the fathers, by means of which Allah gladdened their eyes, by raising their children to them so that they may enjoy seeing them in Paradise. So the verse confirms the other and does not contradict it, because the intended object of the raising is the honouring of the fathers, not the children; the children's benefit is a consequence. In relation to them, it is a bounty from Allah upon them of what is not theirs, just as He bestowed that bounty upon the young boys, the wide-eyed maidens (al-hur al-'in), and the creatures He creates for Paradise. And Allah knows best.

**The Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on Surah 53, Verse 45**

Allah, Exalted and Majestic, says: ﴿And that He created the two mates, the male and the female,﴾ ﴿from a drop of semen when it is emitted.﴾

In this noble verse, He, Exalted and Majestic, mentions that He created the two mates, meaning the two kinds, male and female, from a drop (nutfah), which is the drop of maniyy (semen) when it is emitted, that is, poured out and spilled into the womb, according to the more correct of the two opinions.

The words of Allah, Exalted, support this: ﴿Have you considered the semen you emit? Is it you who create it, or are We the Creator?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 58-59], and His words: ﴿Was he not a drop of semen emitted?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 37].

The Arabs say: amna al-rajulu and mana, when the man emits the semen and pours it out (amna and mana are two verbal forms meaning to emit semen).

Some scholars said: ﴿from a drop when it is emitted﴾ means "when it is measured out (tuqaddar)", in that Allah has decreed that a pregnancy would arise from it. This is from the Arabs' saying: mana al-mani, when he decreed (mana is here used in the sense of decreeing). In this sense is the statement of Abu Qilabah al-Hudhali, and it is said of Suwayd ibn Amir al-Mustaliqi:

*Do not feel safe from death, whether in a sanctuary or outside it,*
*for death's appointed times will reach every person.*

*Take your path in it without shame,*
*until you meet what the Decreer has decreed for you.*

We have already discussed the subject of the drop (nutfah) comprehensively from several aspects, in Surah al-Nahl, in the commentary on His words: ﴿He created man from a drop﴾ [al-Nahl: 4], and in Surah al-Hajj, in the commentary on His words: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection﴾ [al-Hajj: 5]. Each of the two places contains additional material not found in the other.

The argument contained in this noble verse, from the creation of the two kinds, I mean the male and the female, from a drop, has been clarified in other places. It is cited as proof of two matters: the power of Allah to resurrect, and that He created man only so that He might impose obligations upon him and recompense him. Both matters are combined in His words: ﴿Does man think he will be left neglected?﴾ ﴿Was he not a drop of semen emitted?﴾ ﴿Then he became a clinging clot, and He created and proportioned,﴾ ﴿and made of him two mates, male and female.﴾ ﴿Is not He, then, able to give life to the dead?﴾ [al-Hadid: 36-40]. Thus He mentions the proof of resurrection in His words: ﴿Is not He, then, able to give life to the dead?﴾, and He mentions that He did not create him to leave him idle (sudan, meaning neglected) from obligation and recompense, rebuking those who suppose that, with His words: ﴿Does man think he will be left neglected?﴾, that is, left idle (sudan) from obligation and recompense.

We have already presented some discussion of this in Surah al-Furqan, in the commentary on His words: ﴿And it is He who created from water a human being and made him [a relative by] lineage and marriage; and your Lord is ever Competent﴾ [al-Furqan: 54].

[p-473]

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And that it is upon Him that the second creation (al-nash'ah al-ukhra) occurs﴾.

We have already presented the verses that clarify this, and we have referred to them many times.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 53, verse 50:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that He destroyed 'Ad, the first﴾ ﴿and Thamud, so He left none remaining﴾.

We have already mentioned the verses clarifying what He destroyed 'Ad with. As for the verses clarifying what He destroyed Thamud with, they are in Surat Fussilat, in His saying, exalted is He, in the discussion concerning 'Ad: ﴿So We sent upon them a furious wind﴾ [Fussilat: 16], and His saying concerning Thamud: ﴿So the thunderbolt of the humiliating punishment seized them﴾ [Fussilat: 17].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 53, verse 52:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the people of Noah before, indeed they were more unjust and more transgressing.﴾

His saying: ﴿And the people of Noah﴾ is coordinated with His saying: ﴿And that He destroyed the first ʿĀd﴾ [al-Najm: 50], meaning: and He destroyed the people of Noah. He did not explain here the manner of their destruction, but He explained that in other places of His Book (p-474), such as His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the people of Noah, when they denied the messengers, We drowned them﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Furqan: 37].

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years, and the flood seized them while they were wrongdoers﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 14].

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We helped him against the people who denied Our signs. Indeed, they were a people of evil, so We drowned them all﴾ [al-Anbiya': 77].

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Because of their sins they were drowned, then they were made to enter the Fire﴾ [Nuh: 25].

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not address Me concerning those who have wronged; indeed, they are to be drowned﴾ [Hud: 37]. The verses with the like of this are many and well known.

As for what this noble verse includes, that the people of Noah were ﴿more unjust and more transgressing﴾, meaning more severe in injustice and transgression than others, He has explained it in other verses, such as His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed I have invited my people night and day. But my invitation has not increased them except in flight. And indeed, every time I invited them that You might forgive them, they put their fingers into their ears, covered themselves with their garments, persisted, and became arrogant with [great] arrogance"﴾ [Nuh: 5–7].

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Noah said, "My Lord, indeed they have disobeyed me and followed one whose wealth and children increase him not except in loss. And they have plotted a great plot," to His saying: "And they have misled many"﴾ [Nuh: 21–24].

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants and will not beget except a wicked disbeliever﴾ [Nuh: 27].

And His saying: ﴿And he was constructing the ship, and whenever a group of his people passed by him, they mocked him﴾ [Hud: 38].

Among the greatest proofs of this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 14], because a people who were not affected by the call of a noble, sincere prophet over this long period are, without doubt, the most unjust of people and the most transgressing.

Allah's statement: ﴿And the overturned cities He hurled down﴾.

Al-Mu'tafikah (the overturned cities) is a form of ifti'al derived from al-ifk, which means turning over and reversing. What is meant by it is the towns of the people of Lut, as evidenced by His statement in another place: ﴿And the overturned cities﴾ [al-Tawbah: 70], in the plural. This is the use of the singular to mean the plural, as we have clarified many times, and have given many examples of it in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs (p-475), and have referred to it repeatedly. It was called "mu'tafikah" because Jibril (Gabriel) overturned it (afakaha), so it was overturned (i'tafakat). The meaning of afakaha is that he lifted it toward the sky and then turned it over, making its upper part its lower part. Making its high part low is its i'tifak and its ifk.

Allah has clarified this meaning in Surah Hud in His statement: ﴿So when Our command came, We made its highest part its lowest and rained upon it stones of hard clay﴾ [Hud: 82], the verse.

And His statement in Surah al-Hijr: ﴿So the blast seized them at sunrise﴾ ﴿And We made its highest part its lowest and rained upon them stones of hard clay﴾ [al-Hijr: 73-74].

We have explained the story of the people of Lut in Hud and al-Hijr. As for His statement in this noble verse, "ahwa" (hurled down): the Arabs say "hawa al-shay'" (the thing fell) when it descended from high to low, and "ahwaahu ghayruhu" (another caused it to fall) when he cast it from the height to the bottom. Because the angel lifted their towns and then hurled them, that is, cast them, falling toward the earth, with their upper part turned to their lower part.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 53, verse 57:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The Imminent has drawn near﴾.

We have already presented the verses that clarify it at the beginning of Surat an-Nahl, in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ [an-Nahl: 1], and in Surat al-Mu'min, in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And warn them of the Day of the Imminent﴾ [Ghafir: 18].

Allah's statement: ﴿Do you then wonder at this statement?﴾

We have already presented the verses in which the name "ḥadīth" (statement, discourse) is applied to the Qur'an, in Surah at-Ṭūr, in the discussion of His statement: ﴿Then let them produce a statement like it﴾ [at-Ṭūr: 34].
